https://www.shetlandtimes.co.uk/news/cli.text: Home News Article Climate mitigation delegates meet in Shetland, with Seafood Shetland an active participant By Suhani Joshi - suhani.joshi@hnmedia.co.uk Published: 15:00, 26 September 2026 Occam members met in Lerwick last week. Members of a climate change mitigation project met in Shetland last week to discuss “science-based solutions” to help the aquaculture sector. Project partners of Operationalising Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation (Occam), including Shetland Seafood, were in Lerwick for two days in the hope of finding ways to the reduce any environmental impact on the marine sector. Occam is a four year project which has brough in industry, scientists and policy-makers to foster cross-sector collaboration. Delegates discussed the progress of the project - ahead of its 18 month “milestone”. Project manager Freya Robinson said the partners met to take stock of progress across the project, and to plan the next phase of work. She added that holding the meeting in Shetland gave everyone the chance to discuss the work in the context of a working fishing and aquaculture community - rather than around a table in a central European location. "It also allowed us to sample Shetland hospitality at its best, including local music and fine Shetland produce,” said Ms Robinson. Topics for discussion included carp farming in Poland and rainbow trout in Spain, as well as salmon in Faroe and Iceland . The project also ensures economic viability and supports smarter, climate-resilient decision-making throughout the aquaculture value chain. Partners from Norway, Belgium, Denmark, the Faroe Islands, Germany, Iceland, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Scotland are working to find solutions - including the earliest possible detection of harmful algal blooms that may impact shellfish growing in Scottish waters. Chief executive of Seafood Shetland, Ruth Henderson, said she was pleased to be an active participant. “Our seafood industry depends on the natural environment, so it is vitally important that we collaborate with our European partners in aquaculture to share knowledge, adopt best practice, and do what we can to secure a sustainable future,” added Ms Henderson. https://praguemonitor.com/europe-world/c.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Czech motorways need an electronic vignette linked to the number plate; ask whether your rental car already has one before you pay for another (as of 2026; check edalnice.cz). Taking a hire car out of Czechia usually needs the rental firm's permission, and some countries are excluded or carry a surcharge. Czechia has a zero-alcohol limit for drivers, dipped headlights are required all year, and winter tyres are required in winter conditions between 1 November and 31 March (check the Ministry of Transport). On this page 9 sections Do you need a car at all? Licence and documents What the price includes The motorway vignette Taking the car abroad Rules of the road Fuel, charging and parking Returning the car If something goes wrong The price on the booking site and the price at the Prague rental desk are rarely the same. Between them sit a second-driver fee, a waiver to cut the excess, a fuel charge and a question about taking the car abroad. None of it is dishonest if you read the terms, and all of it is easier to handle before you reach the airport. This guide covers what is specific to renting at Prague airport and driving in Czechia. It explains how the system works and does not recommend a rental firm. Do you need a car at all? For a stay in Prague, often not. Trams, metro and buses are dense, parking in the centre is zoned and limited, and the old streets are slow. Our guides to Prague parking zones and driving and low-emission rules in Prague explain the constraints. A car makes sense for castles, spa towns and villages that are awkward by train, and for a family with luggage. Renting at a city branch for just those days avoids paying for parking while the car sits idle. If you want the car from the airport, read on. Licence and documents To rent a car you will need your driving licence, a passport or identity card and, almost always, a credit card in the driver's name for the deposit. Licences issued in EU member states are valid in Czechia. For licences from other countries the position depends on the country and on the rental firm's own policy, and some firms ask for an International Driving Permit alongside a licence that is not in the Latin alphabet. Check your booking terms and the Ministry of Transport's guidance before you travel (as of 2026). Residents face different rules; see our guide to exchanging a foreign driving licence . Minimum ages, minimum licence-holding periods and young-driver charges are contract terms set by each firm, not law. What the price includes The base price almost always includes the compulsory third-party liability insurance that Czech law requires for every car, but not the cover for damage to the rental car itself. Most contracts hold you responsible for a stated excess if the car is damaged or stolen. Firms then offer a waiver to reduce the excess at the desk, usually at a daily rate. Check your own cover first. Some credit cards and travel-insurance policies cover rental excess; read the policy terms and the exclusions. Compare like with like. An online price with the excess waiver included can be better than a cheap price plus the desk upsell. Know the deposit. The firm blocks an amount on your card, which reduces your available credit until the car is returned. Reading a rental quote Line What to check Base rate Per day, with a mileage limit or unlimited? Liability insurance Included by law; check the limits Damage waiver and excess How much do you pay if the car is damaged? Fuel policy Full to full is the simplest; avoid prepaying a tank Extra driver, young driver Daily fees, set by the firm Cross-border Permission and surcharge to leave Czechia Vignette Is the motorway vignette already on the car? Terms differ by firm. Read the contract before you sign. The motorway vignette Czech motorways and many expressways require an electronic vignette, which is registered against the car's number plate. There is no sticker. The vignette is bought online on the official site, edalnice.cz, or at certain points of sale, and a driver without one risks a fine. In 2026 the prices for a passenger car are CZK 230 for one day, CZK 300 for ten days, CZK 480 for 30 days and CZK 2,570 for a year (as of 2026; check edalnice.cz). For a rental car the question is who buys it. Some firms include a valid vignette in the rate, others sell one at the desk and others expect you to buy it yourself. Ask, and check the plate on the vignette matches the car you drive away in. A typing error in the plate number can make the vignette useless. Taking the car abroad Dresden, Vienna and Kraków are all within a day's drive, but rental firms usually want advance notice and may charge a fee. Some countries are excluded in the terms, particularly outside the EU, and others need extra insurance documents. Ask for the written authorisation and keep the rental agreement and vehicle documents in the car. Road charges differ by country. Austria, Slovakia and Switzerland, among others, require their own vignette or toll; Germany does not charge cars for its motorways. Check each country's rules before departure. Rules of the road Speed. The usual limits are 50 km/h in built-up areas, 90 km/h outside them and 130 km/h on motorways, unless signs say otherwise. Speed cameras and section-speed systems are common. Alcohol. The limit for drivers is zero. Do not drive after any alcohol. Lights. Dipped headlights or daytime running lights are required all year, day and night. Winter. In winter conditions between 1 November and 31 March, winter tyres are required (as of 2026; check the Ministry of Transport). Many rental cars are fitted already, but ask. Equipment. A reflective vest, first-aid kit and warning triangle are standard equipment, and rental cars should carry them. Trams. Trams have priority in most situations, and you must not overtake a stopped tram where passengers board from the road. More in our guide to Prague's driving and traffic rules . At the counter Check the contract Confirm the price, the excess, the fuel policy and the vignette against your booking. Inspect the car Walk round the car with the agent and note every scratch. Photograph the car, the fuel gauge and the mileage. Ask about the vignette and winter tyres Confirm the vignette is valid for the plate on the car and ask about tyres between 1 November and 31 March. Know where to return it Check the return point, opening hours and the grace period, and what happens if you arrive after hours. Keep the paperwork Keep the rental agreement, the check-in form and the final receipt until the deposit is released. Fuel, charging and parking Fuel stations label unleaded petrol as Natural 95 (and a higher grade as Natural 98 ), and diesel as nafta . Check the label inside the fuel flap: the wrong fuel is an expensive mistake that the contract will make you pay for. For an electric car, ask the firm which charging cards or apps it supplies, since networks in Czechia use several payment systems. Parking in central Prague is zoned, with permits and time limits, and an unpaid ticket reaches you through the rental firm. Outside the city, castles and trailheads often have free parking, though busy sites fill early on summer weekends. Check the fuel type Natural 95 is petrol and nafta is diesel. The wrong fuel can wreck an engine, and the repair is usually not covered by the damage waiver. Returning the car Return the car with the fuel level the contract requires, and have the agent sign off the condition. Keep the receipt, and photograph the car and the fuel gauge at the drop-off point. Fines for parking or speeding come to the rental firm, which will charge your card an administrative fee and pass your details to the authority. Do not ignore a later letter. If something goes wrong In an accident, make the area safe, call 112 or 158 if there are injuries or a dispute, and phone the rental firm's assistance number. Record the details of the other driver and take photographs. For a complaint about the firm's charges, the Czech Trade Inspection Authority handles consumer complaints. Our explainer on Czech compulsory car insurance shows who pays when a driver is at fault. Frequently asked questions Can I rent a car at Prague airport with a US licence? Most rental firms accept a valid licence from many countries, and some ask for an International Driving Permit. Check the firm's terms and the Ministry of Transport before you travel. Do I need a vignette for a rental car? For Czech motorways, yes. Ask the firm whether one is registered for the car and check the plate. Can I take a rental car to Germany or Austria? Usually, with the firm's permission and sometimes a fee. Austria needs its own vignette. Is it better to rent at the airport or in the city? At the airport if you leave the city straight away. In the city if you spend the first days in Prague, where a car is a nuisance. What is the drink-drive limit in Czechia? Zero. Do not drive after any alcohol. Read the contract before you sign, and photograph the car before you leave the lot. This is a general explainer, not legal, tax or mortgage advice.
